items.text: REFLECTIONS; OR, SENTENCES AND MORAL MAXIMS Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised.
LXVII.--Why we cry out so much against maxims which lay bare the heart of man, is because we fear that our own heart shall be laid bare.

XIV.--The first impulse of joy which we feel at the happiness of our friends arises neither from our natural goodness nor from friendship; it is the result of self-love, which flatters us with being lucky in our own turn, or in reaping something from the good fortune of our friends.
LXXIV.--God has permitted, to punish man for his original sin, that he should be so fond of his self-love, that he should be tormented by it in all the actions of his life.
LIII.--Magnanimity is a noble effort of pride which makes a man master of himself, to make him master of all things.
LXXX.--Few things are needed to make a wise man happy; nothing can make a fool content; that is why most men are miserable.
LIV.--Luxury and too refined a policy in states are a sure presage of their fall, because all parties looking after their own interest turn away from the public good.
XCVII.--Most women do not weep for the loss of a lover to show that they have been loved so much as to show that they are worth being loved.
XII.--Justice in those judges who are moderate is but a love of their place.
III.--Moderation in good fortune is but apprehension of the shame which follows upon haughtiness, or a fear of losing what we have.

VI.--Pride, as if tired of its artifices and its different metamorphoses, after having solely filled the divers parts of the comedy of life, exhibits itself with its natural face, and is discovered by haughtiness; so much so that we may truly say that haughtiness is but the flash and open declaration of pride.
XXXII.--Kings do with men as with pieces of money; they make them bear what value they will, and one is forced to receive them according to their currency value, and not at their true worth.

LV.--Of all passions that which is least known to us is idleness; she is the most ardent and evil of all, although her violence may be insensible, and the evils she causes concealed; if we consider her power attentively we shall find that in all encounters she makes herself mistress of our sentiments, our interests, and our pleasures; like the (fabled) Remora, she can stop the greatest vessels, she is a hidden rock, more dangerous in the most important matters than sudden squalls and the most violent tempests.

XXXIX.--Whatever variety and change appears in the world, we may remark a secret chain, and a regulated order of all time by Providence, which makes everything follow in due rank and fall into its destined course.
X.--Love is to the soul of him who loves, what the soul is to the body which it animates.
LXXI.--The power which women whom we love have over us is greater than that which we have over ourselves.
LXXVII.--The labour of the body frees us from the pains of the mind, and thus makes the poor happy.
XC.--How much is a woman to be pitied who is at the same time possessed of virtue and love!
CVI.--We find very few people of good sense, except those who are of our own opinion.
XXVII.--The praise bestowed upon us is at least useful in rooting us in the practice of virtue.
XLVII.--For us to be always good, others should believe that they cannot behave wickedly to us with impunity.
XLVIII.--A confidence in being able to please is often an infallible means of being displeasing.
LVIII.--It is much easier to take love when one is free, than to get rid of it after having taken it.
LXIV.--We always fear to see those whom we love when we have been flirting with others.
LXXIX.--Humility is the altar upon which God wishes that we should offer him his sacrifices.
LXXXII.--It is more easy to extinguish the first desire than to satisfy those which follow.
XCV.--The greater part of men have qualities which, like those of plants, are discovered by chance.
XCVIII.--There are many virtuous women who are weary of the part they have played.
CIII.--When we love too much it is difficult to discover when we have ceased to be beloved.
CX.--There are certain faults which placed in a good light please more than perfection itself.
CXV.--Those faults are always pardonable that we have the courage to avow.
CXXV.--A man to whom no one is pleasing is much more unhappy than one who pleases nobody.
Moderation is the languor and sloth of the soul, Ambition its activity and heat.
L.--There is a general revolution which changes the tastes of the mind as well as the fortunes of the world.
XCIII.--Good and evil ordinarily come to those who have most of one or the other.
LXXXVIII.--Prudence and love are not made for each other; in the ratio that love increases, prudence diminishes.
CXIV.--It is never more difficult to speak well than when we are ashamed of being silent.
CXVI.--The greatest fault of penetration is not that it goes to the bottom of a matter--but beyond it.
CXVII.--We give advice, but we cannot give the wisdom to profit by it.
LXII.--The most just comparison of love is that of a fever, and we have no power over either, as to its violence or its duration.

LXIX.--It is a common thing to hazard life to escape dishonour; but, when this is done, the actor takes very little pain to make the enterprise succeed in which he is engaged, and certain it is that they who hazard their lives to take a city or to conquer a province are better officers, have more merit, and wider and more useful, views than they who merely expose themselves to vindicate their honour; it is very common to find people of the latter class, very rare to find those of the former.
XXI.--Philosophers, and Seneca above all, have not diminished crimes by their precepts; they have only used them in the building up of pride.
XL.--Intrepidity should sustain the heart in conspiracies in place of valour which alone furnishes all the firmness which is necessary for the perils of war.
XLV.--We do not regret the loss of our friends according to their merits, but according to OUR wants, and the opinion with which we believed we had impressed them of our worth.
LXXVIII.--True penitential sorrows (mortifications) are those which are not known, vanity renders the others easy enough.
VIII.--When we do not find peace of mind (REPOS) in ourselves it is useless to seek it elsewhere.
XVI.--How shall we hope that another person will keep our secret if we do not keep it ourselves.
XX.--One has never less reason than when one despairs of finding it in others.

XXX.--We make no difference in the kinds of anger, although there is that which is light and almost innocent, which arises from warmth of complexion, temperament, and another very criminal, which is, to speak properly, the fury of pride.
XLI.--Those who wish to define victory by her birth will be tempted to imitate the poets, and to call her the Daughter of Heaven, since they cannot find her origin on earth.
XLVI.--It is very hard to separate the general goodness spread all over the world from great cleverness.
XI.--As one is never at liberty to love or to cease from loving, the lover cannot with justice complain of the inconstancy of his mistress, nor she of the fickleness of her lover.

XIX.--The blindness of men is the most dangerous effect of their pride; it seems to nourish and augment it, it deprives us of knowledge of remedies which can solace our miseries and can cure our faults.
XXXIV.--One may say of all our virtues as an Italian poet says of the propriety of women, that it is often merely the art of appearing chaste.

LXI.--The sincerity which lovers and mistresses ask that both should know when they cease to love each other, arises much less from a wish to be warned of the cessation of love, than from a desire to be assured that they are beloved although no one denies it.
LXXXIV.--The great ones of the earth can neither command health of body nor repose of mind, and they buy always at too dear a price the good they can acquire.
